subject: biology
title: DNA, Genes & Variation
welcome_lead: Today you'll meet the molecule that builds you — DNA — and find out why no two people (except identical twins) are exactly alike.
meta_desc: GCSE Biology Inheritance & Evolution intro — DNA double helix, chromosomes, genes, alleles, variation and mutation.
final_note: You learned how DNA is packed into chromosomes, how genes code for traits, and why variation (genetic + environmental) makes every person unique.

concepts.def: Double-helix molecule that stores genetic instructions
A long coiled-up strand of DNA in the nucleus
A section of DNA coding for one protein
A version of a gene (e.g. brown or blue eye)
Differences between individuals of the same species
A random change in the DNA base sequence

walkthroughs.body_html:
DNA is a twisted ladder — a double helix.

It's packed into chromosomes. Humans have 23 pairs = 46 in total.

A gene is a short section of DNA that codes for one protein. Proteins build you.

You get one allele of each gene from mum, one from dad.

Different allele combinations give genetic variation — why siblings look different.

Environmental variation matters too: sun tans skin, food shapes height.

A mutation is a random change in DNA. Most do nothing. Some are harmful. A few are useful.

Useful mutations spread through a population — that's the raw material for evolution.

mcqs.q: How many pairs of chromosomes does a human body cell have?

options: A section of DNA that codes for a protein

numericals.q: If a human body cell has 46 chromosomes, how many chromosomes does a human sperm or egg cell carry?
numericals.hint: Sex cells carry HALF the number — one from each pair

free_texts.q: What is the name for a random change in the DNA base sequence? One word.
free_texts.hint: It's the raw material for evolution
